title: Verifier‑Consistency Estimand: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations (A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study)
abstract: We report a preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; prereg. SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) that tests a narrow estimand: verifier‑consistency under identical inputs. Using a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and template‑synthesized intent→config tasks (N = 120), we produced one canonical LLM candidate per task (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate) and scored it under two conditions: a deterministic template baseline and an LLM guarded condition (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini). All confirmatory episodes completed: baseline = 120/120 verifier passes; guarded = 120/120 verifier passes; paired difference = 0.00; bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We (1) publish the exact execution and scoring artifacts and SHA‑256 fingerprints required for byte‑for‑byte reproduction, (2) show—using those artifacts—why the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics deterministically collapse the paired contrast (identical canonical candidates + deterministic validator), and (3) provide artifact‑grounded runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversification, expanded task heterogeneity) that convert this reproducible pipeline into an informative independent‑reliability benchmark for practitioners. The immutable initial master prompt is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is central to modern NetOps. Operational correctness is safety‑critical: a malformed change can break reachability, violate ACL invariants, or create unsafe transient states during multi‑step workflows. Deterministic offline verifiers (reachability/ACL/routing analyzers) provide auditable, pre‑deployment oracles; pairing fluently generated candidates with such verifiers is the pragmatic path to operational automation. Our preregistered study targeted a narrowly stated estimand: verifier‑consistency under identical inputs ("When the same canonical candidate is given to the deterministic validator under two scoring conditions, does the validator produce different pass/fail outcomes?"). This estimand differs from the operational quantity most practitioners ask—independent generative reliability (the probability an independently sampled LLM output passes a validator). Making the estimand explicit is necessary because experimental generation semantics (shared canonical candidate vs independent per‑condition sampling) deterministically change the inferential target and the appropriate interpretation of results.

Contributions. (i) A fully preregistered, artifact‑complete paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 above) comparing a deterministic template baseline to an LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 synthesized intent→config tasks scored by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. (ii) The exact confirmatory counts and preregistered statistical inference derived from archived traces (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120; paired difference = 0.00; CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0), with file‑level SHA‑256 evidence enabling byte‑for‑byte reproduction. (iii) An artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory contrast is degenerate and precise, runnable recommendations (independent_per_condition, multi‑seed, validator diversification) to convert the pipeline into an informative independent‑reliability evaluation while preserving reproducibility.
sections.related_work:
Verifier‑grounded NetOps evaluation. Deterministic configuration analyzers (Batfish family and successors) are established tools for reachability and ACL validation in pre‑deployment workflows [Brown et al., 2023; doi:10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Contemporary LLM→NetOps research commonly couples fluent generation with deterministic validators and then applies generate–validate–repair loops; design choices about sampling semantics and repair budgets materially affect measured outcomes. Recent empirical studies emphasize that orchestration and feedback design (repair‑loop budget, feedback granularity) can dominate the raw model effect when evaluating repair convergence and success rates (see iterative‑repair literature).

Methodological axes in prior evaluations. Three axes in prior work map directly onto our design choices: (A) sampling semantics: single canonical candidate (shared) vs independent per‑condition or multi‑seed sampling; (B) repair semantics: single‑pass vs bounded iterative repair vs unbounded interactive repair; (C) validator scope: syntactic parsing only vs full reachability/ACL/routing semantic checks vs verifier ensembles. Studies using independent sampling and multi‑seed replications directly estimate independent generative reliability but require larger compute and more archival volume; studies using canonical candidates test validator behavior or pipeline reproducibility.

Why exhaustive artifacts matter. A recurring limitation in some prior work is incomplete artifact publication (missing seeds, missing provider traces, or missing per‑episode validator traces). Our submission includes exhaustive per‑episode provider call traces, canonical response files, and per‑episode validator JSON traces to permit deterministic reruns and external contamination analyses.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen design. The study was preregistered under CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1 (SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea...). The preregistration specified a paired confirmatory design (paired_binary_analysis_v1) across N = 120 tasks (40 per topology class), the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, the deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and confirmatory generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (one canonical LLM candidate generated per task and reused for both scoring conditions). The analysis plan specified a percentile bootstrap (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference CI and an exact two‑sided McNemar test as the confirmatory hypothesis test.

Task generation, templates, and constraints. Tasks were generated programmatically from a deterministic template bank (generator_id deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest entry encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, an explicit required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and workflow_policies (examples: must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups). Templates intentionally include operational transient constraints (make‑before‑break switchover, atomic MTU changes) so the deterministic validator enforces meaningful safety checks. Representative tasks and their full JSON manifests are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 ee55625286dcd27c0a4977043e890054f6456771c202b33c5c9c767233e6568a).

Model, orchestration, and exact accounting. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da...). Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Confirmatory generation semantics: a single canonical candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate) was generated once and reused for both scoring episodes; therefore model_calls_used = 120 despite planned_episode_count = 240. Execution accounting (execution/execution_manifest.json) records: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120, maximum_model_calls = 240. All provider call traces are archived under execution/provider_calls/*.json and the response files under execution/responses/*.txt (examples: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 8f38c8be..., task-000002 shared SHA‑256 ae967f70..., task-000003 shared SHA‑256 f7f4db24...). The counting rule is explicit: when the same generated candidate was reused for multiple scoring episodes, the generation event was logged once and counted toward model_calls_used.

Deterministic validator and scoring rule. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Scoring rule: full_intent_constraint_validation (binary pass requires syntactic parse, enforcement of required_sequence and workflow_policies, transient safety checks, and final_state assertions). Each scoring episode emits a JSON validator trace (execution/scoring/*.json) containing parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, validation_after.final_state and the boolean 'valid'. Representative scoring artifacts: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 0d56c1ad...), execution/scoring/task-000002-guarded.json (SHA‑256 993b8eb3...), execution/scoring/task-000003-guarded.json (SHA‑256 dad1cf4c...).

Confirmatory analysis. Primary estimator: average of (guarded_i − baseline_i) across the 120 paired tasks. Inferential procedures: two‑sided paired Wilcoxon signed‑rank (exploratory) and exact McNemar two‑sided on the 2×2 contingency table; bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference. All analysis code and outputs are archived (analysis/*; e.g., analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 9f25790c..., analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 9c77c96f...).
sections.results:
Execution and confirmatory counts (artifact‑grounded). The run completed as preregistered and all per‑episode artifacts are archived. Confirmatory counts: N = 120 paired tasks; baseline_success_count = 120/120; guarded_success_count = 120/120. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 9f25790c...) is: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (because each canonical candidate was generated once and reused for both conditions). No infrastructure failures occurred (failed_episode_count = 0).

Preregistered inference (artifact matches numbers). Paired difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] from 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All analysis artifacts (CSV tables, bootstrap replicates summary and plot) are archived under analysis/ and match the reported statistics (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 9c77c96f37c4..., analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg SHA‑256 ae5b8e0c...).

Representative validator traces (evidence of deterministic checks). Each scoring JSON shows parsed command counts and the validator’s normalized configuration. Example (task‑000001, guarded scoring JSON): parsed_command_count = 4; required_command_count = 4; validation_after.valid = true; normalized_configuration = the four‑line canonical candidate (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1ad...). The response file used for the pair is execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8be...). Similar per‑task evidence holds for tasks 000002 and 000003 (shared initial SHA‑256 ae967f70..., f7f4db24... respectively) and for all archived tasks 000001–000120.

Why the confirmatory contrast is degenerate (artifact‑visible causal chain). Two preregistered, archived design choices explain the degenerate paired outcome: (1) generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (one canonical LLM candidate generated per task and reused identically for both baseline and guarded scoring episodes; see execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt artifacts), and (2) tight task templates that encode explicit required_sequences and workflow_policies which the canonical candidates intentionally satisfy. Given a deterministic validator, identical inputs yield identical pass/fail outputs, hence n_11 = 120 and the paired difference is necessarily 0. The per‑episode JSON traces and the per‑file SHA‑256 manifest permit exact reconstruction of that causal chain (execution/execution_manifest.json lists every file and its SHA‑256).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and correct inferential scope. The confirmatory statistics correctly answer the preregistered estimand: whether a deterministic validator produces differing pass/fail outcomes for the same canonical candidate under two scoring conditions. They do not measure independent generative reliability (the probability that independently sampled LLM outputs satisfy validator constraints). Conflating these two estimands is a common interpretive error; the artifact bundle makes the distinction auditable.

Runnable, artifact‑grounded modifications (how to answer the independent‑reliability question). Using the archived pipeline one can deterministically rerun informative evaluations without changing the task bank: (A) independent_per_condition confirmatory rerun — generate separate seeds per condition per task (e.g., baseline seed_0, guarded seed_1), rescore with deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and recompute paired contrasts (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2..., execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 ee556252...). (B) multi‑seed confirmatory design — draw K ≥ 3 independent seeds per condition per task and estimate per‑condition pass probabilities with bootstrap CIs. (C) validator diversification — add a second independent verifier and report intersection/union pass rates to reduce validator–task coupling. All files required to perform these reruns deterministically are in the artifact bundle (execution/provider_calls/*.json; execution/responses/*.txt; execution/scoring/*.json). We did not execute these reruns in the reported confirmatory run; they are provided as artifact‑grounded next steps.

Threats to validity (artifact‑documented). Internal validity: shared_initial design removed generation variance by design and therefore precluded testing independent generative reliability. Construct validity: template‑aligned tasks and a single deterministic validator increase the chance that canonical candidates satisfy required_sequences, possibly overstating success relative to open natural language intents. External validity: single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic tasks restrict generalization. Conclusion validity: the degenerate contingency table yields correct but trivial inferential outcomes for the preregistered estimand; caution is required in drawing operational conclusions. All these threats are visible in the archived traces and task manifests and are enumerated in the limitations below.

Practical implications for operators. Two operational takeaways: (1) verifier grounding is essential to obtain auditable pass/fail judgements; (2) experimental sampling semantics must match the deployment question—shared canonical candidates are appropriate for validator reproducibility checks, while independent sampling is required to estimate deployment reliability. Our artifact bundle is intentionally complete so operators can deterministically execute either paradigm and obtain the exact inference they need.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑complete paired experiment and published exhaustive artifacts and SHA‑256 fingerprints enabling exact reproduction. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, both the deterministic template baseline and the gpt‑5‑mini guarded condition passed the deterministic validator on all N = 120 tasks (both 120/120). Archived traces show the causal mechanism: a single canonical candidate per task was reused across conditions and the deterministic validator enforced template‑encoded required_sequences, which yields the observed degenerate contingency. This confirmatory outcome correctly answers the predeclared estimand (verifier‑consistency under identical inputs) but does not estimate independent LLM generative reliability in deployment settings. We provide artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications—independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed replication, and validator diversification—to produce informative independent comparisons while preserving deterministic reproducibility. All artifacts, seeds, provider traces, and validator JSON traces (with per‑file SHA‑256) are included in the submission bundle to support byte‑for‑byte auditing and deterministic reruns.

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: programmatic templates produced narrow required_sequences and workflow_policies that favour canonical solutions and limit external generalizability to heterogeneous operational intents.

Confirmatory shared_initial semantics: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair, reducing independence between conditions and causing the degenerate paired outcome.

Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary analysis used one canonical seed per task; preregistered exploratory multi‑seed analyses were not included in the confirmatory inference reported here.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces constraints encoded in the task templates, which can increase pass rates for template‑aligned candidates and reduce construct validity for open distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: preregistered contamination heuristics found no flags under chosen thresholds, but absence of a flag is not proof of zero exposure to related artifacts in model pretraining.

Single‑model, single‑validator run: results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded configuration and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; they do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or other validators.
